item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c86n4ljxp63o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Three killed after bomb detonated at Moscow restaurant, state media say - Published At least three people have been killed and 21 injured after a homemade explosive device was detonated at an Italian restaurant in Moscow, Russian state media reports, quoting security officials. The blast happened at about 20:00 local time (17:00 GMT) on Kudrinskaya square near the city centre. The National Anti-Terrorist Committee said a woman carrying the explosives tried to enter the restaurant but was stopped by a security guard. The device detonated, killing the woman, the guard and a visitor to the Balzi Rossi restaurant, which had been holding a private function. Authorities have not said who they believe was the target, but many Muscovites will suspect a link to the war in Ukraine. The mayor of Moscow, Sergei Sobyanin, said the blast was "a cruel act of terror which took human lives". He gave no other details, other than to say law-enforcement agencies were working to establish what had happened. In recent years, several senior Russian military figures have been assassinated in and around the Russian capital. Moscow has blamed Kyiv for those attacks. Initial reports said the blast happened in the establishment's kitchen but the restaurant later issued a statement saying "there was a problem outside". The restaurant is located in one of Moscow's famous Stalin-era skyscrapers, with roads around the square briefly closed. Dozens of cyclists had been gathering nearby for an evening ride through the city but the event was cancelled. Video released by Russia's RIA news agency showed heavily armed law enforcement officers at the scene, which had been closed off to members of the public. The Balzi Rossi restaurant apologised on social media for its initial post after the explosion, saying it had been removed "as it was highly inappropriate given the circumstances". State media reported that it had originally posted on Instagram that everything was safe on the premises. The restaurant said it had taken measures to ensure it would not happen again, and said staff were focused on assisting guests and emergency services at the time. - Published1 day ago - Published1 day ago

item.title: 'What was my fault?': How India's exam paper leak ended young lives
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crl7jl1d95eo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'What was my fault?': How India's exam paper leak ended young lives - Published Three days before he was due to sit India's rescheduled medical entrance examination, 17-year-old Kahaan Patel jumped from the sixth floor of his family's apartment building in the western city of Ahmedabad. When his family entered his bedroom after his death in the early hours of 18 June, it looked as though he might return at any moment. His laptop was still open. Text books, notebooks, pens and markers lay scattered across his bed and study table. He was wearing his headphones when he jumped. In one corner stood his electric guitar, plugged into an amplifier. On the shelves were Harry Potter novels, a book on Elon Musk, a collection of Goosebumps horror novels and board games. There was a trophy for "consistent academic performance". "The only thing missing," his father, Prashant Patel, says quietly, "was Kahaan." Kahaan was one of at least 21 students who died by suicide allegedly upset after this year's National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET) was cancelled because of a question paper leak, forcing nearly two million candidates to take the examination again. Their deaths became the emotional core of an extraordinary youth uprising that spilled onto the streets of Delhi in July, where thousands demanded accountability for repeated exam failures. After days of protests led by the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), education minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned. But behind the politics were families like Kahaan's – left trying to understand how an examination scandal had become a matter of life and death. For Prashant Patel, the story begins not with his son's death but with a dream. After scoring well in school leaving exams, Kahaan announced that he wanted to become a doctor. There were no doctors in the family. His parents reorganised their lives around that ambition. They moved from Surat, a diamond and textile hub, to Ahmedabad, Gujarat's largest city, so Kahaan could attend a better school and prepare seriously. His father, a lawyer, bought a flat close to both the high court and Kahaan's school, commuting between the two cities while Kahaan lived with his mother Veena and younger brother Rihaan. "He took that decision himself," his father says. "We only supported him." Kahaan wasn't the sort of teenager consumed only by textbooks. He played football for his school team, devoured Harry Potter and Percy Jackson novels, loved science-fiction films and spent hours teaching himself hard-rock guitar riffs. He had recently secured a US visitor visa and was excited about returning to Disneyland after the exam, revisiting a place he had first seen on a family holiday 12 years earlier. He had already tasted success. After the 2024 paper leak, he took NEET as a practice attempt. His performance convinced both him and his teachers that he was on track. On 3 May, he emerged from the exam convinced he had done enough and called his father. "Daddy, I am so happy. I am feeling free, relaxed. I'm going for dinner with my friends. I'm enjoying." Prashant Patel remembers telling him: "This is your time. Enjoy." Then came news that the paper had been leaked. His parents tried to shield him from the reports, but it was impossible. Friends from his coaching classes were already discussing them. He rushed back from a farmhouse holiday with friends, scrambling to retrieve the notes and textbooks he had already given to younger students in case he had to sit the exam again. Within days the government announced a retest. "That was when he became angry," his father recalls. "He kept asking me: 'Is this a system? Is this how it works? What is my fault? What is the fault of students who gave the exam honestly? Why is the government taking it so casually?'" His father tried to reassure him. "I told him, 'This is the system. What can we do?'" Now he wonders whether his words sounded like comfort or resignation. "Maybe he was disappointed. Maybe he was suffering inside." Nothing suggested a crisis. On the evening of 17 June, the day before he died, Kahaan chatted cheerfully with his grandfather, who had just landed in Melbourne to be with his daughter, on a video call. Kahaan asked him to bring back Puma football boots, Levi's jeans and jackets. Later that evening, he spoke to his father. As the call ended, his father offered one final reassurance: "I told him, 'You proved yourself once. You don't have to prove yourself again.'" Hours later, he was dead. Only afterwards did friends tell his father how deeply the examination scandal had unsettled him. "He kept asking why the people responsible couldn't take the right decisions," his father says. "He used to say, 'Is this a joke for our ministers to conduct examinations like this?'" Kahaan's family was not alone in asking those questions. Some 770km away, in Rajasthan's Jhunjhunu district, another family was trying to understand an equally unimaginable loss. Pradeep Kumar was 23. His father, Rajesh Kumar, is a small farmer in a village where Pradeep was the only student preparing for NEET. Rajesh, 45, had left school as a child. His wife had never been to school. Becoming a doctor would have made Pradeep one of the first in the family to climb into the professional middle class. "He would tell me, 'I want to serve people so much that they will remember me,'" Rajesh says. To finance that dream, he sold land and borrowed more than a million rupees ($10,480; £7,804) from a bank. Coaching in Sikar, one of India's biggest hubs for entrance exam coaching, cost a fortune. In 2022, Pradeep moved to Sikar for coaching, sharing a rented room with his older sister, Babita Kumari who was preparing for police recruitment exams. Two NEET attempts steadily improved his rank, bringing a government medical college within reach. Then came his third attempt in May this year. The paper was leaked, the examination was scrapped and a retest ordered – meaning Pradeep would have had to sit NEET for a fourth time. By then, his life was a relentless 16-hour cycle: up at 4.30am, coaching, self-study until 9pm, sleep, and repeat. Everything else was stripped away. Pradeep refused to own even a mobile phone. "I'll buy one after I'm selected," he would tell his father. "Phones distract me." His only indulgence was a collection of about 10 inexpensive wristwatches, bought from roadside shops on trips between Sikar and home. After sitting the exam on 3 May, he emerged smiling. "This time my selection is guaranteed," he told his father. The family planned to leave Sikar, return to their village and celebrate. Instead, the paper leak surfaced. "We'll have to prepare again," Pradeep told his father stoically. On the morning of 15 May, Rajesh did what he had done almost every day for four years. He sent milk and homemade curd to Sikar on the morning bus. Pradeep phoned to say it had arrived. He bought fresh okra from a roadside vendor and told his sister, "Go and have your bath. When you come back, we'll cook." When she returned half an hour later, the room was locked. In the time she had been away, her brother had taken his own life. "He never told me anything," Rajesh says. "He seemed happy." His voice hardens when he speaks about the leak. "I sold my land to educate him. Those who have money buy question papers. Those who study honestly are left behind." Then he says something that has consumed him ever since. "The government snatched away my son. If the paper had not leaked, Pradeep would be alive today. He would have been celebrating." Kahaand and Pradeep came from different Indias. One was the son of a lawyer who split his week between two cities. The other was the son of a farmer who mortgaged his future for his child's education. One dreamed of Disneyland after NEET. The other postponed buying a mobile phone until he became a doctor. Yet both fathers are left asking the same question: how did children who believed they had earned their future lose faith in the very system meant to reward them? For weeks after Kahaan's funeral, Prashant Patel struggled to emerge from grief. What finally drew him out was the students. He travelled to Delhi twice to join their protests in July. "I wasn't there for compensation," he says. "I wanted accountability." Weeks of protests forced education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation on 25 July. The government expressed sympathy for the families of students who died by suicide and promised "maximum compensation in accordance with the rules and regulations". But for Prashant Patel, the real legacy of the movement lay elsewhere. He had watched students return to the streets after police action on 20 July. "I wanted to thank them because they had become Kahaan's voice. If these children can come back after being beaten and still fight for justice," he says, "that gives me strength." His son never found that voice. "Kahaan didn't speak out," he says. "Instead, he took his own life." He pauses. "The other children spoke." Then he says the words he wishes every parent – and every government – would hear. "Our duty is to hear the voices of the young before they fall silent."

item.title: A bruising 24 hours - what next for Fifa and under-pressure Infantino?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/c9w0djx2g92o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
A bruising 24 hours - what next for Fifa and under-pressure Infantino? - Published A week is a long time in politics. Football politics. On Tuesday morning, Gianni Infantino was in an impregnable position as Fifa president, the most powerful job in football. Now, after trying to sell stakes in Fifa competitions to private investments firms - apparently without the knowledge of anyone else - Infantino's position appears to be under threat. Uefa - Infantino's fiercest critic - dealt its trump card on Thursday by threatening to boycott all Fifa competitions, including the World Cup. Now European football's governing body senses the opportunity to remove Infantino - and this is likely to be the best chance it will ever get. But they're far from the only unhappy federation. Concacaf, the confederation Infantino worked so closely with to organise the 2026 World Cup, has called for a "full review" into the leadership of Fifa in light of Infantino's plan. Even more damaging, loyal countries in the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) shunned him too. Then he was abandoned by two of his closest allies - first senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro and then chief operating officer Kevin Lamour. After Infantino backtracked in the early hours of Saturday morning, Uefa delivered another devastating blow by issuing a strong statement saying it had lost confidence in him. The battles lines have been drawn. What could happen next? - Uefa has 'lost confidence' in Infantino's Fifa leadership - Published1 day ago - Four reasons why Fifa's World Cup plan never stacked up - Published1 day ago - Infantino on the brink? Who might replace him if he goes? - Published1 day ago How could Infantino be ousted? The quickest route for Infantino's exit would be for the Swiss to resign, like his predecessor Sepp Blatter did in 2015. But Infantino still retains support and he could try to hold out until March, when he is up for re-election for a fourth and final term as president. What other avenues are open? The Fifa Council could try to force Infantino's hand through an emergency meeting. Such a gathering would be triggered if 19 of the 37 Fifa Council members call for one. Uefa has nine members, AFC has seven, Concacaf five, Africa has six, Conmebol five and Oceania three. It is completed by Infantino and secretary general Mattias Grafstrom. BBC Sport understands there are some doubts that the 19 votes could be achieved. If they do get to 19, the meeting must take place within two weeks and the Fifa Council could call on Infantino to tender his resignation. But he could simply refuse to do so. It would, however, add further pressure. The next step would be an extraordinary congress of the 211 Fifa member associations, which would be held if one-fifth, or 43 associations, "make such a request in writing". So Uefa, which has 55 nations, can trigger the extraordinary congress whenever it wishes. That would take a minimum of two months from the point it is triggered, but more likely three months, and there is no guarantee of success. In effect, it would be a de facto election without there being another candidate as 106 votes would be needed to pass the vote of no confidence. Uefa has 55, Africa 54, Asia 46, Concacaf 35, Oceania 11 and Conmebol 10. Africa, Conmebol and Oceania have not criticised Infantino's plan. So could Uefa get to 106? In total, 136 countries officially rejected the investment plan, but voting to reject an idea is not the same as voting to kick Infantino out. Of the 136, Qatar have already publicly backed him and Mexico have distanced themselves from the joint Concacaf statement. Which leaves finding a suitable candidate to fight the election in March. Infantino stood unopposed when he was re-elected in 2019 and 2023 and if someone wants to battle him for the position, the deadline to announce their candidacy is 18 November. - The five dramatic days that shook Infantino and world football - Published1 day ago Who could potentially replace Infantino? If Uefa and Infantino's biggest critics have to go down the election route, they will need to find a unifying leader. As Uefa has been so strong in its opposition to Infantino, a European candidate might struggle to get global support. After all, it might seem like it is trying to take over Fifa itself. So there must be a candidate who can attract the support of those countries in Concacaf, Africa and Asia who could have been loyal to Infantino but could be persuaded to switch their votes. The most likely candidate appears to be Concacaf president Victor Montagliani. Like Infantino, he was elected in 2016 promising governance reform. A former president of Canada Soccer, Montagliani was heavily involved in the build up to and delivery of the 2026 World Cup. He is fluent in French, Italian and Spanish, as well as English. Another option would be Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa, the AFC president. Initially elected in 2013, he was re-elected unopposed for a fourth term to run to 2027. Sheikh Salman signed off the confederation's brutal takedown of how Fifa is being run by Infantino and has carried with him a 46-member confederation, many of whom are aware the figures being offered by Infantino's plan are huge in terms of their overall football expenditure. Less likely appears to be Paris St-Germain president Nasser Al-Khelaifi, the Qatari who is also the chair of European Football Clubs. Al-Khelaifi helped bring European football back together after another seismic event that threatened to pull the game apart - the ill-fated European Super League. In theory, the Qatari would be a serious challenger to Infantino. But it seems he doesn't want the role. Qatar's support for Infantino could be an issue, too. How likely is it that Infantino is ousted? In any other business, Infantino would be unlikely to continue in his role. But football, of course, is not a normal business. Remember, Blatter had been re-elected the week before he resigned in 2015 when he had no option left amid a corruption scandal. So will Infantino try to fight on? In his statement on Saturday, he said his intent "was to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks". For Infantino, contrition could make this all float away. Maybe it is working. Following on from Qatar, 2030 co-hosts Morocco backed him on Saturday evening. Then Egypt praised Infantino for cancelling his masterplan. Infantino may be thinking that if he can, day by day, get more member associations on board, the prospect of a no-confidence vote is less likely to be successful. After all, his support base has been so strong for so long you can understand why he might have such faith. As any vote of no confidence is three months away, he has the chance to repair at least some of the damage. It is a race to 106 - and the more time elapses, the more chance Infantino can persuade his former allies this was just an aberration. For Uefa, the question is whether it can create a situation whereby Infantino is left with no option but to resign. For that to happen, the criticism from federations across the world must continue. But if there is one thing that could damage Infantino further, it would be for major sponsors to distance themselves from the organisation. During the 2015 Fifa scandal, Sony, Emirates, Castrol, Continental Tyres and Johnson & Johnson were among the companies to discontinue their huge sponsorship deals. There is no sign of this just yet but this is a saga with the potential to rumble on. Related topics - Published8 June - Published8 June

item.title: How Spain's migrant crisis created a political storm - whipped up by social media
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62vl925dqdo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
How Spain's migrant crisis created a political storm - whipped up by social media - Published Most of the tens of thousands of migrants who swam into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta on Thursday have now returned to Morocco, escorted to the border by Spanish soldiers and police. But the extraordinary surge of arrivals has left at least 72 people dead, their bodies pulled from the sea where they floated alongside abandoned rubber rings and flippers. This week's events have also shaken Europe politically, once again exposing divisions over the sensitive issue of migration. And they've left lingering questions about what sparked the sudden influx: whether social media posts promising an easy path to Europe just went viral or this was something more deliberate, even organised. The politics Whatever the cause, Spain's socialist prime minister is angry with the response. Pedro Sanchez has hit out at some in the EU for "attacking" Spain in this crisis, playing politics instead of showing support. He meant Italy, above all. Fratelli d'Italia, the hard-right party of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, had been quick to post images of migrants racing through the streets of Ceuta. "This is the Sanchez model the Italian left wing likes so much," the caption crowed. Meloni then announced she was suspending Italy's Schengen agreement with Spain that allows for the free movement of people, citing a security threat. Madrid is fuming. The way Spain sees it, the crisis has been contained and Ceuta is not in the Schengen zone so Moroccan migrants were never going to head for mainland Europe, unchecked. Meloni knows that. But she faces elections next year with her coalition losing ground to a new and virulently anti-immigrant party. This was a chance to sound tough herself and claw back votes and she leaped on it. Soft touch Spain? Italy is not the only country to see Spain as soft on migration, though. Meloni's call for an urgent meeting of interior ministers to be held on Tuesday was signed by almost two dozen EU heads of state, calling for the elimination of all policies that could be "pull factors" to Europe. Above all, they mean Spain's controversial move to allow hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrants apply for residence and work permits and "regularise" their status. The government's pragmatic: Spain is ageing and needs workers. But those who flocked to the beaches of Ceuta this week were not heading to sign up for a campaign that's already closed. Sanchez himself points instead to a recent ruling by Spain's Supreme Court: it said those who enter by sea cannot be pushed back immediately. The prime minister argues that was misrepresented by smugglers to promise an easy path to Europe. The crowd heading for Ceuta didn't need to pay smugglers, though, because most were Moroccan and the route is well known. The message was actually spread online. Migrants have shown social media posts to reporters with people shouting that "Spain is Open" and jumping into the sea. Multiple accounts we've checked ourselves show young people in wetsuits and flippers, or filming themselves already swimming, mixed with pictures from inside Ceuta itself. Some have only been active for weeks. Several have tens of thousands of likes. All their promises were false. The crowds who made it to kiss the shore in Ceuta with joy were met with nothing. Without food or shelter, and with no way on to continental Europe, most quickly turned back. So what was it all about? So have migrants been "weaponised" as happened a few years back in Belarus, for example? If so, who did it? For now we only see those enjoying the results. The global right wing are "hyperventilating with happiness", as journalist Andrea Rizzi wrote in Spain's El Pais newspaper. US President Donald Trump, angry at Spain for opposing his war on Iran, has talked of a "catastrophe" and an "invasion". Like Meloni, he has an election looming. Russia has been gloating, too: it loves chaos and division in Europe. Anything to weaken Ukraine's allies. As for Morocco, it's blaming "criminal organisations". But its border guards must have seen the crowds building. The last time something similar happened, albeit smaller, Spain and Morocco were at loggerheads over Western Sahara, a former colony. There are new tensions, right now. Sanchez is emphatically not blaming Morocco for what happened, calling Rabat a "good ally". But his critics call that appeasement and say he should be "showing teeth". Results For now, Spain is busy protecting Ceuta against further incident. It is extending the border fence out to sea, attaching long lines of orange buoys to the jetty which ships will then patrol to deter future swimmers. Next week, EU interior ministers will talk about strengthening external borders, with those on the populist right emboldened. Travellers from Spain to Italy face random document checks by police for a few weeks. So no huge change. Except for the dozens of young people who set out to sea, chasing a vision they'd seen online, and are now being sent back to Morocco in coffins. - Published1 day ago - Published2 days ago - Published2 days ago

item.title: How Australia combines modern tech and Indigenous knowledge to fight wildfires
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czdmvr984yyo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
How Australia combines modern tech and Indigenous knowledge to fight wildfires - Published The wildfires currently ravaging Europe feel close to home for Professor Marta Yebra, despite being on the other side of the world. Originally from Spain, the Canberra-based bushfire expert has spent years developing ways for Australia - home to some of the most fire-prone landscapes in the world - to battle its own blazes. She heads up the Bushfire Research Centre of Excellence, which was set up in the aftermath of Australia's worst fire season on record: the Black Summer fires of 2019-20, which razed a combined area about the size of the UK. Her team looks at how technology such as satellites, drones and AI can be used to better detect fires, alongside the knowledge of experienced firefighters. Equally important, though, is the knowledge and experience that has accrued in Australia over thousands of years, and has been passed down through generations. This is where Australia has an advantage. The use of fire has been part of the country's Indigenous culture since long before Europeans arrived in the 18th century - but the value of this ingrained knowledge has only been truly realised in recent years. From outer space to underground Yebra has spearheaded an innovative project, bringing together millennia-old knowledge in Australia's Indigenous communities with cutting-edge satellite imagery to help detect where fires are most likely to break out. The satellite images pick up the "fuel moisture content" in the landscape, which signals where there might be a large amount of fuel, such as dry leaves, grass, shrubs and bark. But such data provides just one part of a bigger picture. That's where the likes of Adrian Webster come in. Growing up on the south coast of New South Wales (NSW), Webster learnt how to read the environment or "country" - the term Indigenous Australians use for their ancestral homeland – from his elders. Using Indigenous ecological knowledge – a plant's colour and scent, for example, or the shade cover of trees - he can verify information in the satellite images from Yebra's team. "She had all this amazing data, but there was no translation to what it meant on the ground, so it was kind of useless," he explains. "But through an Indigenous perspective, it was not useless. It was a map that could guide you through the country and, if you understood it, take you directly into a place that is ready to burn." For Webster, assessing the land involves him "literally digging and going underground," he says. "We're looking at the subsurface level and then everything from that up beyond the canopy." Yebra said there was a "remarkable agreement" between Webster's local knowledge and the satellite data, demonstrating the combined value of Indigenous expertise and Western science. Her team now hopes to get more funding for the project, and work with Indigenous communities to co-design plans to protect the land and manage fires. For Webster, it's about "allowing our mother – the planet Earth – a voice again". Fire as friend, not just foe Another example of ancient wisdom influencing modern techniques can be found in the way Australia fights fire with fire. Cultural burning refers to a longstanding practice by Indigenous Australians to manage the environment while also maintaining a deep, spiritual connection to the land. Part of it is lighting "cool fires": small, controlled blazes that create a patchy landscape, so fuel does not build up in one area. "In Europe, there is no such cultural aspect to this kind of landscape planning," Yebra says. Wildfire scientists in Spain have blamed a massive build-up of fuel for the blazes currently devastating the country. "It is difficult to watch what is happening in Spain, but it is not surprising," Yebra says. "Particularly as climate change is increasing the frequency of extreme fire weather across southern Europe." She believes Europe, facing its worst wildfires in decades, could benefit from Australia's firefighting experience. "We have decades of experience living with large and high-intensity bushfires," she says. "One of the biggest changes we are seeing in bushfire management is a shift from simply reacting to fires towards anticipating risk and acting earlier. "The earlier we can identify risk or detect an ignition, the more options firefighters have." Webster says a key lesson the world could learn from Australia is "don't sit back and wait". "The longer you leave it, the more fuel there is to burn, so the fire is naturally going to be bigger and harder to extinguish," he says. "Indigenous people always knew that, so we burnt continuously all the time. That way there was no fuel for big fires." The practice of lighting cool fires dates back 60,000 years. Part of Webster's role is to assess the area before one is lit, looking for natural signs of oil and water in the landscape so that the blaze remains under control. "All the answers are in the environment," he says. "There's a sweet spot in the middle where there's enough water to slow that fire down but there's enough oil to push that fire on." A more modern tactic used across Australia is a prescribed burn, also known as a hazard reduction burn. These carefully planned, often large-scale fires are usually carried out during cooler months, and are increasingly being adopted in parts of Europe. It's an approach that has become especially vital in the "urban fringes", says superintendent Andrew Shurety from Fire and Rescue NSW. As Australia's population grows and suburbs expand, more people are moving closer to bushland, making hazard burns firefighters' "main mitigating factor that we try to do to reduce the risk of bushfires because we know they're going to come". The problem, Shurety points out, is that longer fire seasons and more rain during cooler months shortens the window that such burns can be carried out. Starving a fire of fuel is also the idea behind "backburning", a widely accepted practice in Australia where a blaze is deliberately lit ahead of a main fire to strip out the vegetation and try to stop it from spreading. This approach is also being increasingly adopted overseas - as Queensland firefighter Damian Hatfield found out. When he travelled to Alberta, Canada with a contingent of Australian firefighters to help tackle the country's worst wildfires on record, backburning was not widely used. A year later, things had shifted. "Backburning was definitely much more at the forefront when I returned in 2024," he says, with Canadian firefighters showing "no hesitation" to include the approach in their operations. Drones have also transformed how Australia deals with bushfires, says Trent Curtin, from the Rural Fire Service in NSW - particularly in recent years. "The local crews arrive, send a drone up quickly, have a look at where the fire is and how it's progressing, get some intelligence and make decisions before we can even get our large helicopters or other aircraft down," Curtin explains. Drones also deliver heavy gear to crews on the ground, start blazes for backburning operations and help assess the damage caused by fires. The summer ahead Back at Yebra's centre, the team's work is particularly timely with weather forecasters predicting a super El Nino this summer - which could increase the probability of extreme heat, drought and bushfires. "Our next fire season is looking like it's going to be a bad one," Yebra says. That concern is shared by Jason Heffernan, chief officer of the Country Fire Authority in Australia's southeastern state of Victoria. Here, the memories of 2009's Black Saturday bushfires – the country's deadliest on record – loom large. "For this summer coming, we're bracing for what could be something extremely significant," Heffernan says. Even in the broader scheme of things, he notes that local fire seasons are starting earlier and lasting longer. "Unfortunately for Australia", he adds, "our environment is designed to burn." But as the world braces for wildfires that are more frequent and intense, Heffernan also believes "we must take a global perspective". "No fire service can do this on their own and the key is to have formal and trusted networks," he says - as well as national and international resource-sharing arrangements. One of the challenges as a fire chief, he explains, is knowing when to ask for help - too late and the benefits will be lost, but too early and resources might be wasted. Such a call was made just earlier this week, when France sent its first-ever request for help from Australian firefighters. Two dozen crew and several aircraft will be deployed as France battles record-breaking wildfires amid a prolonged summer heatwave. Australia regularly sends specialist teams to the US and Canada, and vice versa, with many requests for what's known as "arduous fire crews": those who have fought fires in rugged and remote areas. There are far fewer requests from Europe, Heffernan says - but this may change as "the global fire community is becoming more connected". As he points out, while forests and climates vary across the globe, "we're seeing bushfires occur in parts of the world that never had bushfires before". - Published1 day ago - Published11 June

item.title: Solitude as a new aspirational lifestyle: 'We are not lonely'
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y63dw2x3wo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Solitude as a new aspirational lifestyle: 'We are not lonely' - Published It's a Friday night. A young woman trudges back to her apartment after a day of work. She enters a spotless kitchen, unloads a bag of groceries, and unwraps a frozen pizza before sliding it in the oven. What follows is a nightly routine that is almost meditative in its mundanity: she lights a candle and gazes briefly at the snow-covered landscape outside her window, piles a premade salad onto a plate with the pizza, and settles on her sofa to eat in front of the TV. The tagline that accompanies the scene reads: "POV you're a childfree and single girl that has no friends and lives alone so this is how you spend your Friday night." At the centre of the video – which has amassed seven million views on TikTok – is Lana Isa, a software sales manager in her 20s based in Toronto. In addition to chronicling her nightly self-care routines, she takes her almost 400,000 followers across TikTok and Instagram on late-night fast food drives, reading sessions perched on a rock by the lake, even a saga of getting locked out of her apartment in the middle of the night. Isa is part of a growing, albeit niche corner of the internet where content creators, many of them women, share their daily rituals of living alone, choosing to spotlight a lifestyle that prioritises peace and solitude - the antithesis of social media excess. For Isa, unveiling the "no friends" aspect of her life was less of a tagline, but the "reality" she had been living for several years. Alone, but not lonely After switching several high schools, enduring Covid isolation during her college years and moving across the country following her first heartbreak, Isa found herself forced to adjust to living alone with no close friends. "People don't talk about having no friends a lot... I think it's still what people would consider embarrassing or a little taboo," she says. When she started sharing the friendlessness of her circumstances on social media, an audience began to connect. Her initial following of around 2,000 followers on TikTok swelled to more than 175,000 in the span of eight months. "It was eye-opening to see other people who are living the same situation that I've been… and to feel like I could kind of relate to people for the first time in a while." And relate they did. Isa's comments section filled with people bonding over similar experiences of living alone or having no friends, and finding comfort in "feeling seen". As with most trends online, curiosity quickly turned to backlash. Isa and similar creators were dubbed "loneliness influencers", with some framing them as part of a new demographic of sad, lonely, childless women in crisis. Others accused them of romanticising self isolation and encouraging an "air of cosy defeatism" by shunning social connections. But their reels paint a lifestyle that may be more relatable than many would care to admit. These women take themselves on solo dates, embark on spontaneous road trips, and even push through the awkwardness of attending parties alone. Destigmatising loneliness For Devon Noehring, a full-time content creator and self-proclaimed introvert based in Phoenix, Arizona, it's been "frustrating" to see her solo weekends cooking and lounging at home with her dog reduced to a symptom of female loneliness. "It's the exact opposite intention of our videos," she says. "I just hate the stigma of alone equalling lonely." While Noehring does have a close group of friends, growing up she always felt "ashamed" of being the quiet girl with social anxiety. It wasn't until she confessed her insecurities online that she discovered a following of fellow introverts who identified with her struggles. "Being alone is where I feel my most free and most like myself," she says. "That's how I recharge, and I feel very proud of myself for being independent and doing things alone… I think it's something that should be celebrated." Some health researchers have been working to "destigmatise loneliness" by differentiating between chronic loneliness forced by circumstance and those who have agency to choose to live and spend time alone. "Everybody's lonely at some point, but some people are not OK admitting that," says Professor Melody Ding, an epidemiologist researching social connection and loneliness at the University of Sydney. "That can create this false expectation that you have to be socially happy and connected all the time." But she cautions that while influencers can make being alone look "really appealing", humans still need social connection and it can be detrimental to one's mental and physical wellbeing to be stuck in a cycle of intense isolation. "We're a social species," says Ding. "We survive better with companionship, with people around us." She acknowledges that people's social needs vary at different stages of life, but Ding's hope for those who have lost relationships is that they can eventually "de-emphasise" the friendless aspect of their lives and forge new social bonds. "It's important we have people in our life and it's important these relationships are positive and nourish our lives," Ding adds. 'We want to find people we relate to' Even in moments when they do feel lonely, these women say loneliness doesn't define their lives, nor do they aspire to remain permanently friendless. "We never describe ourselves as lonely," says SJ Hoadley, who works as a cleaner in the UK and began documenting her own solo living after discovering Isa's videos. "I think sometimes my lack of friends tends to bother the people around me more than it bothers me." After leaving a seven-year abusive relationship, she moved to a new area where she knew no one and was confronted with having to rebuild her life. Despite the initial "shock", she eventually started "enjoying and embracing that independence" and "getting to feel comfortable with my own company". In a social media ecosystem that thrives on flooding our feeds with aspirational living and a perennial state of FOMO (fear of missing out), the rise of solo living influencers can be validating for those who see themselves reflected in the lifestyle, says Dr Anne Oeldorf-Hirsch at the University of Connecticut who specialises in how humans build community online. "There's been this kind of long growing backlash against the idea that we're seeing everybody's perfect life, their highlight reel," she says. Oeldorf-Hirsch believes the appeal of solitude content is filling a social need for the creators and their audience, providing some "balance" against the dominance of hyper-glamourised influencer culture. "We're kind of trending towards these influencers that are more authentic, living their true life," she says. "We just want to find people we relate to." Hoadley has seen her following surge at times by tens of thousands per day, while Noehring's videos have garnered millions of views across her channels. Those online connections have made Hoadley excited for a future where she finds a "little group of girlfriends". Noehring hopes to one day organise a real world meet-up with her virtual community, and Isa says the support has given her the "push" she needed to start thinking about making friends again. "I think that what all the content is saying is: find your path," says Hoadley. "It doesn't have to be this one-size-fits-all that we keep getting pushed on social media."

item.title: Ginger hair portraits show unexpected 'golden thread' connecting Americans
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce97nyz4rvmo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Ginger hair portraits show unexpected 'golden thread' connecting Americans - Published For Kieran Dodds, photographing people with red hair has become something of an obsession over the past decade. The 45-year-old, from Edinburgh, who is himself a "proud ginger", began taking pictures in his homeland in 2013 as part of a series examining Scottish identity. His interest in the subject soon took him to other ginger hotspots such the Russian city of Perm and Jamaica's Treasure Beach. His 2020 book Gingers spanned the world but after its release he noticed there was a "huge gap". "I realised I didn't have any American citizens," Kieran told the BBC. "Then all these people got in touch." "I was like 'oh wow, of course, the whole world is in the States'," Kieran says. "It's a microcosm." He says a message from a Native American man who had red hair instantly aroused his curiosity. "I found it very interesting and it made me think, 'where on earth did it come from?'" The cover of his latest book - Gingers of America, external - features Joshua Elliot from the Muscogee (Creek) Nation in Oklahoma. He told Kieran that some of his mother's relatives were German and on his dad's side there were people from England and Sweden, so that could explain where his ginger hair comes from. "My mom's side has always been involved with the Muscogee tribe and traditions and I've grown up around it," he said. Joshua knows he does not fit people's expectations of what a Native American should look like, but he said: "Our chief's wife told me it's about your involvement in your community and your tribe, the people around you and what you put back into it. "Which I really took to heart." Kieran spoke to a lot of Native Americans on his visits and most knew of a European ancestry which could explain their red hair. "The thing that surprised me was how early on there were these Scots and Irish marrying Native Americans," he said. Lottie Wahkinney, a Comanche girl from Oklahoma, has Scottish grandparents, from Hawick. Her father Jared told Kieran his dad was Comanche but his mum was born and raised in Scotland. "That's why my Lottie has a good mix of everything going on," Jared said. "My Scottish grandparents would come over every summer. "On my first visit to Scotland when I was 22, folks were like, 'Where are your moccasins? Where's your headdress?'. "I explained 'I wear Nikes'." While most Native Americans could explain where the ginger gene might have come from, there was one exception - a Cherokee girl called Lakia - whose family knew of no European ancestry. "It is a totally different colour of red," Kieran said. "It's deep ruby. That really intrigued me." In the book, Lakia says that all her family, on both sides, have jet-black straight hair but hers turned red during her childhood. "Everyone thought, since I was about eight, that I dyed my hair," she said. "And still now everyone's like, 'what hair colour is that?'." After meeting Native Americans, Kieran knew there was something in the US he could explore. Over the next few years, he made seven lengthy trips, often linked to his full-time profession as an environmental photographer. One state he found surprising was Alabama, a place many in the UK associate with racial segregation and the struggle for civil rights as well as its pioneering space exploration programmes. "I knew it for racism and Nasa," Kieran said. "In my head it was stuck in the 60s but Birmingham is an incredibly vibrant city. "I met a lot of black Americans who had often married someone who is white." Rachel Releford told Kieran that when she goes out with her daughter Liliana people think she is the nanny or the babysitter. "I'm like, 'nope, she's mine'," Rachel said. "I think you still get some people who grew up with the mindset that things need to be segregated. "Some of my grandparents' friends were a little hesitant when they found out I was dating my husband. They said: 'You're really going to let her date someone of a different race?' "But my grandparents were like, 'Go for it. He's a cool guy, he's a sweet one.' I love him for who he is. He's a great human being." Also in Alabama, he met Henry Davis and his young son Henry Davis II. The older man no longer has any red hair but he says he looked just like his son when he was the same age. "We're not really sure where it comes from," Henry senior said. "My dad is turning grey now. He'll get some red in his beard, and then it kind of goes grey. "So I guess it's from his side." As someone who grew up with red hair himself, Kieran says he is well aware that ginger can be used as an insult. However, he says: "I use the word for its descriptive power because red is the colour of fire engines and blood whereas ginger has a golden tone to it. "You can use it in a kind way." He says the book uses ginger hair as "a golden thread" that weaves together America's diverse and difficult history in a way which shows a connection between people. "That's my big idea," Kieran says. "We are all made of the same stuff and with the ginger hair it shows." According to Kieran no-one exemplifies this better than a young lad named Cali whom he met in Alabama. "His background is everything - European, African-American, Hispanic and indigenous as well," he says. "His gran is white but she was unable to get married to a black guy in Alabama - even after the courts had made it legal. "She moved to Georgia and had a family there. It's an incredibly diverse family." In Scotland, it is thought as many as 13% of the population - about 700,000 people - are natural redheads, a higher percentage than anywhere else in the world. Globally, less than 2% of the population are thought to have red hair but Kieran's research lead him to believe the US figure is higher than that. "We landed on about 4% for the genetic prevalence," he says. "If all the gingers in America were gathered in one place, Gingertown would be about 14 million people. "It's a big city. You would see it from space it would be so bright." Kieran says the big difference between America and other places is that they tend to have really thought about where they come from. "Everyone has self-consciously moved from somewhere," he says. "And that includes the Native Americans, who have been moved from other parts of America. "That's what makes it interesting." He says his book is a road trip through the US trying to find out about the country through this unique trait. For Kieran, the recent men's football World Cup got people excited about the US again in a way they haven't been over the past few years because of political divisions. He says he was pleased to see people visiting the US and saying "it is not what I expected". "There's such a lot of amazing people and communities there," he says. "People you might connect with and agree with on a lot of things. "I'm quite heartened that the football has revealed that. "I feel quite patriotic for America now."

item.title: Death row inmates desperate to escape execution in Saudi Arabia call the BBC
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c80nkgdnl4no?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Death row inmates desperate to escape execution in Saudi Arabia call the BBC - Published There was desperation in the voice of the young Ethiopian man when he managed to get through to the BBC from a phone in his prison cell on death row in Saudi Arabia. Habtom, whose name - like the other prisoner featured in this article - has been changed to protect his identity, has been held in a jail in the southern city of Khamis Mushait for more than three years. Above the noise of cellmates shouting behind him, he pleaded for help and sounded angry that his government appeared to be doing little to change his fate. "One prisoner cannot comfort another. We have no choice but to cry. We are waiting for our turn, even though we do not know when it will happen," said Habtom. He and some of his fellow inmates had fled war and poverty at home in the hope of finding a better life. But that quest, which took him through Djibouti and Yemen, led to his incarceration - joining a growing number of Ethiopians in Saudi prisons who face the prospect of execution for drug-smuggling offences. Anxious to tell their story, some of the prisoners managed to get hold of the mobile phone number for the BBC's Tigrinya language service. In total we have spoken to seven of the dozens - perhaps as many as 200 - Ethiopians inside the prison who are waiting for a death sentence to be carried out. Other foreigners, including Pakistanis, Sudanese and Jordanians, are in a similar position, but in the first seven months of this year 17 Ethiopians have been executed - the highest number among non-Saudis. Five of those executions happened on Monday. Two years ago, according to research by Amnesty International, just two Ethiopians were executed, but 35 were put to death in 2025. It is not clear exactly why there has been an uptick, but it could be linked to more people leaving the northern Ethiopian region of Tigray, where a brutal two-year civil war in Tigray ended in late 2022, leaving devastation in its wake. "It may also be linked to Saudi Arabia's expanding use of the death penalty for drug-related offences in recent years," Amnesty International researcher Dana Ahmed tells the BBC. Habtom, who like most of those the BBC spoke to is from Tigray, was found guilty of smuggling hashish, a type of cannabis. In Saudi Arabia, on the judge's discretion, a guilty verdict can result in a death sentence. But rights groups - including Reprieve, Human Rights Watch (HRW) and Amnesty International - have said that in these kinds of cases due process is rarely followed. Defendants are not given access to a lawyer or the court papers - while translation, when it is offered, can be inadequate, Amnesty's Ahmed says. Although there is the theoretical right to appeal, without a lawyer they cannot submit one "and then the sentence is automatically upheld", she says. "There is a near-total lack of transparency throughout the entire judicial process, from sentencing to Supreme Court review and ratification by the King. People on death row and their families are left in the dark about their fate." Habtom alleged that he was not given the chance to speak to a lawyer or defend himself. He also said he was forced to sign a document in Arabic, which said he agreed to the sentence, without understanding what he was putting his name to. Other prisoners that the BBC spoke to had similar stories about the legal system. HRW has also contacted people close to the cases and learned about "mass sentences, mass trials that lacked any kind of due process and people detained then just waiting with no idea when the sentence would happen", Nadia Hardman, the organisation's senior adviser on refugee and migrant rights, said. The Saudi authorities did not respond to a BBC request for comment on allegations that the legal process was not fair, but every execution is accompanied by a statement issued through the official press agency. It outlines a clear process: an investigation, a court case, an appeal, a Supreme Court ruling and then a royal decree. The sentence reflects the commitment to protect citizens "from the scourge of drugs" and the damage they can cause, the statement adds. Habtom said that although he manged to keep in occasional contact with his family via the wall-mounted phone in his prison cell, he refused to tell them he was on death row: "I would rather they be told after I die than now." He had dreamt of finishing high school, graduating from college and getting a job to support his parents - but the Tigray war put paid to that. "My goal was destroyed, so I decided to emigrate," he said. After surviving the dangerous journey to Saudi Arabia in 2021, Habtom found low-paid work as a goatherder, but his employers offered him and others a chance to earn more money. They were asked to deliver a package but were stopped by police on the way and were found with the narcotic leaf known as khat - a natural stimulant that is widely used in the Horn of Africa. The official Saudi statements all refer to hashish smuggling but those the BBC spoke to talked about khat. "I did not know what we were carrying. But later I was told it was khat. I don't even know what khat is," Habtom said, admitting that he was tempted into the work by the sum of money on offer. Habtom acknowledged he had "made a mistake without knowing it" and hoped that his sentence could be commuted to prison time. Three of his fellow Ethiopian detainees were executed in April - another nine were killed in June. The April killings sparked an outcry from rights groups and some leading Ethiopian figures, including the influential head of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. Patriarch Abune Mathias urged the government to negotiate with the Saudi authorities and called the inmates "voiceless children" living "under the shadow of death". In its April report, HRW called on the Saudi authorities to immediately halt executions of Ethiopian migrants and ensure all cases were handled in line with international law. It also asked Ethiopia's foreign ministry to intervene urgently and provide consular support. The safety of Ethiopians in general in Saudi Arabia was raised at a meeting in Addis Ababa in May between Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos and Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister Waleed Al-Khuraiji. This was followed in June by a visit to the prison by Ethiopia's Ambassador Tafa Tulu Dadi, though the prisoners told the BBC that they were not given enough time to explain their situation to him. It also appeared to have limited impact as in the following week more Ethiopians were executed. The African Union's human rights commission has also urged Ethiopia to safeguard the lives of Ethiopians facing execution in Saudi Arabia. The BBC has contacted Ethiopian officials in Saudi Arabia and the government in Addis Ababa for comment but has not received a response. Without referring to the death penalty specifically, Ethiopia's foreign ministry did release a statement on 13 July saying it was in regular contact with the Saudi authorities "pursuing appropriate remedies for Ethiopian citizens facing difficult circumstances". It added that "to date" nearly 2,000 Ethiopians had "benefited from royal amnesties" - without mentioning the crimes or sentences. As they await the outcome of diplomatic manoeuvres, the prisoners who spoke to the BBC said they were enduring hardships in overcrowded facilities. Desta, located in another part of the prison, said there were 200 men in his cell crammed into an area designed for 90 people, with 45 bunk beds arranged around the walls. During the day, the prisoners sat on the floor in stifling conditions squeezed up next to one another; when the temperature dropped at night, they covered themselves with rubbish bags in lieu of bed sheets, he said. "The stress of facing execution, combined with the overcrowded conditions, exposes us to illness and anxiety," Desta said. "The guard only opens the door to bring food, covering his mouth and nose with a mask - that is the only time the door is opened. After he gives us the food, he quickly locks it and leaves. "It is not possible to ask them any questions or speak to them. Even if you ask, there is severe beating." He was arrested while trying to cross the border from Yemen more than three years ago and accused of smuggling drugs. "We were four Ethiopians, and there was one Yemeni with us. He told us he could help us cross the border safely because he knew the safest route. In return, he asked us to carry packages containing khat and even promised to pay us some money. "Unfortunately, shortly after we crossed, we were captured by police officers. They opened fire on us, and the Yemeni man ran away, but we couldn't. We were shocked and had no idea where to go." Like all those interviewed by the BBC, Desta said he had never expected to be sentenced to death and believed he would eventually return home after serving time in prison. Instead, he alleged that he was also forced to sign a document in Arabic that listed charges carrying capital punishment. Later, when he appeared in court, he said that he was denied the chance to challenge the charges and had no legal representation. "When you appear before the judge on the first day, he asks: 'Do you accept the charges?' On the second appearance, he sentences you to death," Desta said. As a brick-maker struggling to support his family, he had left Tigray during the war as the fighting edged closer to his home. Now he worries for his life again - and he, Habtom and dozens of others on death row are begging for outside help. "We are living in deep fear and cannot even eat the food we are given," said Habtom. At the scene of deadly Moscow bomb blast At least three people have been killed and 21 injured after a homemade explosive device was detonated at an Italian restaurant in Moscow, Russian state media reports, quoting security officials. The blast happened at about 20:00 local time (17:00 GMT) on Kudrinskaya square near the city centre. The National Anti-Terrorist Committee said a woman carrying the explosives tried to enter the restaurant, which was holding a private event, but was stopped by a security guard. The BBC's Russia editor Steve Rosenberg reports from the scene in Moscow, where the explosion happened. item.title: Fastest runner to cross the Alps says it was an incredible experience
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/crk5j6g8lmko?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Fastest runner to cross the Alps says it was an incredible experience Runner Sophie Woods became the fastest person to complete the 2,000km (1242-mile) Via Alpina ultramarathon beating both the men's and women's record. Woods ran the route through storms, heat of up to 37C and dodged floods and wildfires across eight countries. "Through the whole thing, I was only ever thinking about the day, the hour, the sort of minute that I was in", the runner told BBC Breakfast. The previous record was 35 days and Woods did it in just 29, crediting ice cream slushies for helping her power through. Wildfires scorch Washington state as thousands evacuated and emergency declared Wildfires across more than 250,000 acres have forced evacuations and caused power outages in the Washington state's Spokane area, US officials said. Washington State Governor Bob Ferguson declared a statewide emergency and burn ban on Saturday morning. "Our state is facing a very serious situation with multiple fires, and our hearts go out to Washingtonians who are losing their homes", Ferguson said. According to officials, no injuries or fatalities have been reported. Spokane is the state's second most populous city. item.description:

Crowds line Amsterdam's canals for Pride boat parade Amsterdam came alive with music, colour and celebration on Saturday, as thousands of people flocked to the canals to watch the city's annual Pride boat parade. The Dutch capital is hosting this years' WorldPride event, drawing visitors from across the world. Costumed participants danced and waved from a colourful flotilla of 80 decorated vessels as they made their way through the city's waterways. Security was visibly heightened at the event, with police cruising the canals in motorboats. The measures come just a week after a deadly attack on a Pride event in Berlin, which killed one person and injured at least 29 others.
